article_title: Start Making a Reader Today® (SMART®) (Beginning Reading)
citation: What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. (2007). What Works Clearinghouse Intervention Report: Start Making a Reader Today® (SMART®). https://www.getsmartoregon.org
title: SMART® four-strategy volunteer tutoring pattern: reading to, reading with, re-reading, and questioning
description: The SMART® program structures minimal-training volunteer tutoring around four reading strategies: "reading to the child, reading with the child, re-reading with the child, and asking the child questions about what has been read." A volunteer handbook describes these strategies, and volunteers rely on their own judgment for any other needs. The pattern intentionally places minimal demands on volunteer tutors and classroom teachers, with training focusing as much on tutoring logistics as on reading instruction techniques.
requirements: A volunteer handbook describing the four reading strategies
1–2 hours of volunteer training, preferably before the school year begins
constraints: The program intentionally requires minimal training, so volunteers rely on their own judgment beyond the four strategies
target_learners: First- and second-grade students at risk of reading failure
target_learning_goals: Reading engagement, fluency, and comprehension through one-on-one reading interaction
examples: Volunteers tutor students one-on-one for 30 minutes twice a week throughout the school year using these four strategies.
key_sources: What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. (2007). What Works Clearinghouse Intervention Report: Start Making a Reader Today® (SMART®). https://www.getsmartoregon.org

article_title: Pre-K Mathematics with DLM Early Childhood Express Math
citation: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, What Works Clearinghouse. (2013). Pre-K Mathematics with DLM Early Childhood Express Math. http://whatworks.ed.gov
title: Teacher-guided small-group manipulatives lessons paired with parallel take-home parent activities
description: The Pre-K Mathematics program organizes instruction as weekly math activities presented twice in teacher-guided small-group lessons of four to six children lasting approximately 20 minutes, using concrete manipulatives, with "related math activities... sent home every 1 to 2 weeks" and parents encouraged to engage their children with these activities. Home activity materials parallel the classroom activities and are available with picture strips in English or Spanish. This classroom-plus-home structure was implemented across both reviewed studies over the school year.
requirements: Teachers need the core program package (teacher's curriculum book, Activity Aid Masters, Home Activity Masters, and Assessment Record Sheets) and training; in the reviewed studies teachers received multi-day workshops and ongoing on-site training approximately twice per month.
constraints: The pattern was evaluated as a supplement to existing general curricula (The Creative Curriculum, High/Scope, Montessori, or local curricula), not as a stand-alone replacement.
target_learners: preschool children in Head Start and state-funded preschool classrooms
target_learning_goals: early mathematical knowledge in counting, arithmetic, geometry, patterns, measurement, and logical reasoning
examples: In the PCER study, 29 classroom activities were completed and teachers sent 19 home activities and materials for children to complete at home, with teachers completing Assessment Record Sheets tied to each session.
key_sources: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, What Works Clearinghouse. (2013). Pre-K Mathematics with DLM Early Childhood Express Math. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/InterventionReport/381

article_title: Scholastic RISE and RISE Up
citation: Schechter et al. (2024). Scholastic RISE and RISE Up program evaluation, Florida district, 2022-2023 school year.
title: Small-group station rotation for Tier 2 reading intervention
description: The program organizes intervention as rotation of small groups of four students through instructional stations. In RISE, "groups of four students rotate through four instruction stations for 45-60 minutes per day for six to eight weeks"; RISE Up uses three stations focused on comprehension strategies on a short text for 45 minutes a day. The rotation distributes explicit, structured instruction across comprehension, word study, phonics, and writing.
requirements: Groups of four students
45-60 minutes per day
Six to eight weeks of implementation
Teacher(s) or interventionists staffing the stations
constraints: RISE coaches provided guidance to modify the program for a 30-minute day timeframe with one instructor to meet the district's intervention model
target_learners: Students in grades 1-5 reading below grade level (Tier 2)
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension
word-solving
fluency
writing
examples: RISE stations leveled C-N target comprehension, word-solving, fluency, and writing; RISE Up stations leveled O-Z focus on comprehension strategies on short texts

article_title: JUMP Math
citation: JUMP Math — Evidence Rating: Promising. (2023). https://www.jumpmath.org
title: Reduce math concepts to small steps to mastery, then build back up incrementally
description: In JUMP Math, "Math concepts are reduced to increasingly smaller steps until students achieve mastery, then built back up incrementally to meet the curriculum demands." Students receive extensive practice at each step. This stepwise reduction-and-rebuild structure is the core instructional mechanism of the program's guided-discovery approach.
requirements: Extensive practice at each step before moving on
target_learners: K to 8 students
target_learning_goals: mastering math concepts and meeting curriculum demands
examples: The program's teachers guides move students towards discovering target concepts through the sequence of small steps.

article_title: Rapid Cycle Pilots: Improving Ed-Tech Products through Feedback
citation: Gadgil, S., & Louw, M. (2016). Rapid Cycle Pilots: Improving Ed-Tech Products through Feedback. Learning Media Design Center, Carnegie Mellon University. Report to Digital Promise. http://www.digitalpromise.org
title: Run small, targeted pilots confined to one grade level or subject area to identify suitable ed-tech products
description: When districts pilot ed-tech products to generate local efficacy evidence, the report recommends keeping pilots small to medium-sized and focused on a single grade level or subject area. Such pilots "were likely to be more targeted, and resulted in successfully identifying suitable products, compared to pilots that tested products over a multitude of grade-levels and subject areas." The report also stresses thorough needs-analysis and goal alignment between district needs and the product's intended use as preconditions for a meaningful pilot.
requirements: A thorough needs-analysis before choosing the product
Goal alignment between the district's instructional or curricular needs and the product's intended use
Clear communication of goals and objectives with all stakeholders, with buy-in from teachers and administrators
constraints: Product implementation and pilot success were inhibited by technological issues, timely roll out of products, and device limitations in some cases
target_learners: School and district leaders planning ed-tech adoption; K-12 students in pilot classrooms
target_learning_goals: Generating usable local evidence of ed-tech product effectiveness to inform purchasing decisions
examples: Avonworth piloted eSpark in six first-grade ELA classrooms and Puzzlets in one classroom each of grades K-2; Elizabeth Forward piloted the Amplify games suite across twenty-four grade 6-8 classrooms

description: The guide's fourth recommendation is to "create small, personalized communities to facilitate monitoring and support" in schools with many at-risk students. Implementation steps include deciding whether communities serve single or multiple grades, creating teacher teams that share common groups of students, identifying a theme to build identity and engagement, and scheduling common planning time for staff to monitor students. article_title: Teaching Academic Content and Literacy to English Learners in Elementary and Middle School
citation: Baker, S., Geva, E., Kieffer, M. J., Lesaux, N., Linan-Thompson, S., Morris, J., Proctor, C. P., & Russell, R. (2014). Teaching Academic Content and Literacy to English Learners in Elementary and Middle School. What Works Clearinghouse Practice Guide. https://www.whatworks.ed.gov
title: Select a small set of academic vocabulary words for in-depth instruction using explicit selection criteria
description: Rather than teaching every unfamiliar word, educators should choose a small set of academic vocabulary for in-depth instruction. The guide's selection matrix screens candidate words against criteria: whether the word is "Frequently used in the text", "Central to understanding the text", "Appears in other content areas", has useful "Affixes", "Multiple meanings and uses", and "Cross-language potential". In the worked zoo-text example, words like environment, exhibit, impact, investigation, option, and pursuit were screened this way.

constraints: Schools with strict district-mandated curricula may need to use existing resources and publicly available complex texts

target_learning_goals: Academic vocabulary knowledge supporting content-area comprehension
examples: The guide's Step 2 matrix screens six candidate words from a zoo-design informational text against the six criteria

constraints: Component offerings vary by site, with three sites medical-only

article_title: Cultivating Relationships in Secondary Schools: Structures That Matter
citation: Hernández, L., & Darling-Hammond, L. (with Nielsen, N.). (2024). Cultivating relationships in secondary schools: Structures that matter. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/cultivating-relationships-secondary-schools-brief
title: Small learning communities: cohorts/houses, advisory systems, looping, and block scheduling that keep students and staff together in smaller units
description: Small learning communities organize staff and students into 'smaller and closer-knit units' and are described as 'a primary mechanism for promoting personalized relationships in schools.' The brief enumerates four options for large comprehensive secondary schools: cohort/house structures, advisory systems, looping across more than one year, and block scheduling with fewer, longer class periods. Each is intended to create the conditions under which students can be known well by consistent adults.
requirements: Cohorts should ideally be much smaller than typical houses of 300 to 600 students, with 80 to 120 students identified as ideal
In effective advisory systems, each advisor serves a small group of students (usually 15–20), often over 2 to 4 years, meeting regularly and acting as liaison between school, student, and home
Block scheduling fosters relationship-building especially when courses continue for a full year and teachers use longer periods for inquiry, directed practice, and personalized instruction
constraints: Some houses in large comprehensive schools contain 300 to 600 students, which the brief treats as larger than ideal
target_learners: secondary school students
recently immigrated newcomer students
target_learning_goals: student motivation, engagement, and sense of being known by school adults
academic, social, and emotional development
examples: Vista High School houses 100–130 students sharing a set of four core teachers and one special education teacher
Oakland International High School keeps an interdisciplinary team of four core teachers with 80–100 students for 2 years, alongside advisories

article_title: Studying Circular Motion with an AI-Generated Smartphone Physics Lab
citation: Josep Ll. Suñer, Francisco M. Muñoz-Pérez, Juan C. Castro-Palacio, Juan A. Monsoriu, Martín Monteiro, Cecilia Stari, and Arturo C. Martí. (2026). Uniform and Accelerated Circular Motion with a Smartphone: A No-Code, AI-Generated Browser Laboratory. https://smartphysics.webs.upv.es/rotation-lab
title: SmartPhysics: Rotation Lab — a single-file, no-installation, AI-generated browser application for measuring rotational motion
description: SmartPhysics: Rotation Lab is a single self-contained HTML file requiring no installation, developed in one conversational session with Claude Sonnet 4.6 through natural-language prompting, with no code written or edited by hand. It reads the device's gyroscope and orientation sensors via the DeviceOrientation and DeviceMotion Web APIs, plots orientation angles and angular velocity components live, supports zoom and pan, and exports data as CSV and screen captures as PNG. Measurements reported used a Redmi Note 13 Pro 5G in Google Chrome at a 50 Hz sampling rate.
requirements: A mobile browser exposing the DeviceOrientationEvent and DeviceMotionEvent interfaces and a page served over HTTPS; on iOS, sensor access must be granted through an explicit user gesture
constraints: Desktop browsers, and mobile browsers that do not expose the motion sensors, load the interface but record no data
target_learners: introductory physics students
target_learning_goals: measuring and verifying rotational kinematics (angular position, angular velocity, angular acceleration)
examples: The consolidated prompt used to regenerate the application and the generated HTML file are provided as supplementary material

article_title: Pedagogical Safety in Educational Reinforcement Learning
citation: Oluseyi Olukolaa, Nick Rahimia. (2026). Pedagogical Safety in Educational Reinforcement Learning: Formalizing and Detecting Reward Hacking in AI Tutoring Systems. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.04237
title: SmartTutor simulated Python tutoring testbed for evaluating pedagogical safety in educational RL
description: SmartTutor is a simulated Python tutoring environment comprising "a knowledge graph of 27 Python concepts (DAG, max depth 7", a student model with per-concept mastery tracking, a neural contextual bandit agent with UCB action selection over a 124-dimensional state representation, an action selection module enforcing C1 and C3 online, and a configurable reward system. Eight pedagogical actions span cognitive demand from d=0.0 (Encourage) to d=1.0 (Challenge), with Encourage producing zero mastery gain but the largest engagement boost (+0.8). Three learner profiles (Struggling, Average, Advanced) vary initial knowledge, gain multiplier, and confusion threshold.
requirements: A knowledge graph of prerequisite relationships, a student mastery model, and a configurable reward system with engagement, mastery, and pedagogical-appropriateness components
constraints: Simulated learners use a heuristic mastery update rather than full BKT inference and do not capture motivation, fatigue, or off-task behavior
The single domain (Python programming) limits generalizability to other subjects and curricula
target_learners: Simulated programming learners (struggling, average, advanced profiles)
target_learning_goals: Mastery of Python programming concepts
examples: Each main condition ran 30 sessions (3 profiles × 10 random seeds × 150 interactions per session), yielding 4,500 interactions per condition and 18,000 total across main conditions
key_sources: Oluseyi Olukolaa, Nick Rahimia. (2026). Pedagogical Safety in Educational Reinforcement Learning: Formalizing and Detecting Reward Hacking in AI Tutoring Systems. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.04237

article_title: Estimating Item Difficulty Using Large Language Models and Tree-Based Machine Learning Algorithms
citation: Pooya Razavi, Sonya Powers. (2025). Estimating Item Difficulty Using Large Language Models and Tree-Based Machine Learning Algorithms. Edmentum. https://www.edmentum.com
title: SME-elicited feature set for LLM item evaluation, combining domain-general and domain-specific cognitive and linguistic features
description: A catalog of item features developed through focus groups with four subject matter experts from the assessment design team and cross-referenced with prior literature, then rated by GPT-4o for each item. The process yielded "both domain-general features, which SMEs considered relevant to both subjects (e.g., Cognitive Load, Depth of Knowledge), and domain-specific features (e.g., Symbolic Reasoning for math; Figurative Language for reading)". Math items were rated on 20 targeted questions and reading items on 13, using numeric (e.g., 1-10), binary (Y/N), and DOK (1-4) scales, plus a holistic 1-100 overall difficulty rating. These ratings served as predictors in the tree-based models.
requirements: SME focus groups grounded in the specific item pool to identify difficulty-relevant features
LLM prompts specifying response options or ranges for each feature
constraints: One math feature (evaluating someone else's calculations) was excluded for near-zero variance
Features already available as item metadata (grade level, domain, word count, item type) were excluded from the LLM rating task
target_learners: K-5 students taking mathematics and reading assessments
target_learning_goals: Accurate estimation of item difficulty for adaptive assessment and item development
examples: Four SMEs with at least five years of K-12 assessment design experience participated in two one-hour video-conference focus groups (a math dyad and a reading triad), costing approximately two hours each.

article_title: Paradigms of shared knowledge
citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2009). Paradigms of shared knowledge. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-009-9075-7
title: SMALLab mixed-reality design pivots on three principles: face-to-face interaction, distributed thought and action, and immediate consolidation
description: The SMALLab mixed-reality classroom design, presented by Birchfield and Megowan-Romanowicz, pivots on three principles: direct face-to-face interaction among co-located participants should be cultivated; thought and action should be distributed across multiple participants through an active, generative process unfolding in real time; and immediate spatial and temporal consolidation of emergent conceptual models should follow the active learning process. The editorial states each principle "supports shared knowledge" by providing preconditions and mechanisms for knowledge sharing through structured interaction.
requirements: Computationally mediated space with projection of virtual reality into the physical classroom interacting with student behaviors
target_learners: Whole classrooms of students, including at-risk students
target_learning_goals: Construction of scientific shared knowledge of abstract earth sciences concepts
examples: The reported study demonstrates that situating groups of students in the mixed-reality setting can be highly motivating even for at-risk students

citation: Joep van der Graaf, Michelle Taub, Yizhou Fan. (2023). Introduction to special issue on facilitating self-regulated learning with scaffolds: Recent advances and future directions. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09364-9
title: SMA-grid and what/when/how/by-whom-or-what frameworks for characterizing SRL scaffolds
description: The introduction uses two frameworks to compare the special-issue studies. The SMA-grid (Molenaar et al., 2023) characterizes each study by CAMM processes (Cognition, Affect, Metacognition, Motivation), data streams (physiological, behavioral, contextual), and analytical approach (unimodal, horizontal, vertical, integrated). Alongside it, the what, when, how, and by whom or what of scaffolding (Azevedo & Jacobson, 2008) distinguishes what to scaffold, when to provide a scaffold, how it is delivered, and the delivery mechanism. Together these axes organize the seven contributions' similarities and differences.

constraints: The introduction notes the contributions focus on the C and M of CAMM, one data stream, and log-file data, so the grid's affect/motivation and multimodal cells are barely exercised in this issue

secondary students
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning
metacognition
examples: Table 1 classifies each of the six contributions by CAMM processes, data stream(s), who, when, how, and whom or what, e.g., Dever et al.: log data and questionnaires, during learning, pedagogical agents, rule-based, log-informed

article_title: Self-Regulated Learning, Multimodal Data, and Analysis Grid: Where Are We Now and Where Are We Going?
citation: Joni Lämsä, Susanne de Mooij, Martine Baars, Inge Molenaar, Sanna Järvelä. (2026). Self-Regulated Learning, Multimodal Data, and Analysis Grid: Where Are We Now and Where Are We Going? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10113-4
title: The SMA grid as a framework for mapping SRL measurement across CAMM processes, data streams, and analytical approaches
description: The self-regulated learning, multimodal data, and analysis grid (SMA grid) organizes how studies measure SRL by relating CAMM processes to data streams and analysis approaches. The article states that "The self-regulated learning, multimodal data, and analysis grid (SMA) is used as a framework for mapping and analyzing these processes across diverse data streams." It distinguishes unimodal, horizontal, vertical, and integrated approaches to combining data streams, and reveals that affective and motivational processes receive less attention than cognitive and metacognitive ones.

constraints: The grid shows temporal aspects of affective and motivational processes have gained little attention in LA and AI measurement of SRL
target_learners: Learners in digital and technology-enhanced learning environments
target_learning_goals: Self-regulated learning across cognitive, affective, metacognitive, and motivational processes
examples: The special issue's five contributions map their studies onto the SMA grid, including reviews of motivation and mind wandering and two empirical studies.

article_title: Transforming Self-regulated Learning – Multimodal Insights and Future Directions
citation: Tina Seufert. (2026). Transforming Self-regulated Learning – Multimodal Insights and Future Directions. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10119-6
title: SMA Grid: a two-dimensional classificatory framework for multimodal SRL research
description: The Self-regulated learning, Multimodal data and Analysis Grid (SMA Grid) is a classificatory and organizing framework for multimodal SRL research, with one dimension differentiating cognitive, metacognitive, affective, and motivational (CAMM) components and a second dimension characterizing multimodal measurements. The paper states it "serves as a valuable tool for structuring the rapidly growing field of multimodal SRL research," promoting transparency, comparability, and conceptual orientation. It functions from heuristic classification to guiding analytic design, but does not claim to be a fully developed theoretical model of SRL.
requirements: Theoretical grounding is the responsibility of the individual study, since the grid remains open to various theoretical interpretations.
constraints: The grid does not provide a fully developed theoretical model of SRL; it supports existing frameworks by visualizing how modalities and process components connect.
target_learners: Researchers and designers of learning environments studying self-regulated learning
target_learning_goals: Understanding and classifying how self-regulated learning is measured and analyzed with multimodal data
examples: The reviews by de Mooij et al. and Bühler et al. systematically used the SMA Grid to classify studies; Kubsch et al. exemplify one of the few genuinely integrative applications within the Topical Collection.

article_title: A Systematic Review of Self-Regulated Learning through Integration of Multimodal Data and Artificial Intelligence
citation: Susanne de Mooij, Joni Lämsä, Lyn Lim, Olli Aksela, Shruti Athavale, Inti Bistolfi, Flora Jin, Tongguang Li, Roger Azevedo, Maria Bannert, Dragan Gašević, Sanna Järvelä, Inge Molenaar. (2025). A Systematic Review of Self-Regulated Learning through Integration of Multimodal Data and Artificial Intelligence. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10028-0
title: The SMA grid: a two-dimensional framework mapping CAMM processes against data streams and four analytic approaches
description: The Self-Regulated Learning Processes, Multimodal Data, and Analysis (SMA) grid, introduced by Molenaar et al. (2023) and applied in this review, maps SRL research along two axes: CAMM processes (cognition, metacognition, affective states, motivation) and data streams (behavioural, physiological, contextual). It distinguishes four analytic approaches: "The unimodal approach is a classical approach, focusing on a single CAMM process with one data stream", horizontal (multiple processes, one stream), vertical (one process, multiple streams), and integrated (multiple streams, multiple processes). The review mapped 141 studies onto the grid to visualise typical combinations.
requirements: Studies must report process data capturing the sequence and timing of events during a learning task and apply process-oriented analysis to be mappable onto the grid
constraints: The review notes prior data taxonomies (Di Mitri et al. 2018; Sailer et al. 2024) are insufficiently granular for SRL-model-specific characteristics

description: The article recommends integrating SMS as a learning support tool in higher education, particularly in developing countries where mobile phones are popular and require less infrastructure investment than computers and internet. Its evidence shows SMS added to traditional face-to-face instruction "was more effective to improve students' learning than relying on only in-class instruction". description: The article argues that science topics contain abstract concepts students find difficult, and that learning is more permanent when activities appeal to more senses: "when many senses are used in an educational activity, the rate of recall is increased". title: SMART design as a method for developing adaptive interventions with sequential randomization
description: The sequential multiple assignment randomized trial is a design in which "participants are randomly assigned to intervention components at multiple stages of the intervention," with assignments determined by decision rules based on proximal outcomes. Participants meeting a benchmark are deemed responders and continue unchanged; nonresponders receive preassigned modifications. Head-to-head comparisons across the multistage randomization yield "embedded interventions" whose most promising version can proceed to future research. The article uses it to compare two context-personalization approaches and two nonresponder supports.
requirements: Random assignment at each phase, with at least one round determined by an intermediate tailoring variable indicating response to Stage 1 components
constraints: The article notes a standard RCT makes it difficult to identify what works for whom, motivating the SMART approach

target_learning_goals: reading comprehension during summer months
examples: Stage 1 randomized students to CCT + App or LT + App; Stage 2 randomized nonresponders to augment-only (gamification) or augment-and-intensify (gamification plus text messages) supports

description: The article recommends SMS messaging as an add-on support tool for EFL courses, following So's recommendation to "employ basic and trusted technologies such as SMS to connect with our students". Feedback on answers should be provided, ideally the same day

Cost of SMS exchange may prevent learner participation until flat rates and free messaging apps are widespread

title: SMS mini-lesson design: short, immediate, self-contained exercises with same-day feedback

target_learning_goals: vocabulary learning and retention of language rules
examples: SMS 1 introduced bored/boring with a short text and rule, SMS 2 asked a one-word choice question, and SMS 4 returned feedback reusing the words in context

constraints: The pedagogy focuses on small-group scaffolding specifically due to limited conditions in the EFL context, such as limited authentic immersion resources and test-oriented learning goals

reading comprehension strategy use
active English learning attitudes

citation: Meng Ya, Song Jian, Yu Xiaojing, Xu Xiaoxia, Zhang Hao. (2023). Design and evaluation of blended teaching in the smart classroom combined with virtual simulation training in basic nursing courses. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04721-3
title: Blended basic-nursing teaching design combining smart classroom, virtual simulation training, and peer-assisted learning
description: An instructional design for basic nursing courses that, in the article's words, "involved combining theoretical teaching with virtual simulation training and PAL; engaging in online and offline hybrid teaching". It comprises preclass microclasses and task sheets on an online platform, in-class Rain Classroom quizzes and interactions, post-theory virtual simulation laboratory practice, paired PAL scoring via QR-coded electronic score sheets, and summary feedback. The article evaluates it against traditional lecture teaching in a quasi-experimental study of 135 nursing undergraduates.
requirements: Smart classroom hardware and network: interactive whiteboards and screens, movable desks, Wi-Fi high-density coverage
Recorded microclasses and clinical cases, an online platform with WeChat groups, and a virtual simulation training system with imported student information
A PAL scoring sheet with QR codes and the PAL app for paired operation exercises
constraints: The article notes smart classrooms have high requirements for classroom facilities and network speeds, and that many teaching designs cannot be implemented if these are not met
The design places a higher burden on teachers
target_learners: Undergraduate nursing students in basic nursing courses
target_learning_goals: Theoretical and practical nursing knowledge and skills
Independent learning ability
examples: Experimental-group students practiced enemas, catheterization, and cardiopulmonary resuscitation in the virtual simulation laboratory, then formed random pairs in the nursing practice room, scanning QR codes through the PAL app to supervise and score each other's operations

title: Implement smart-classroom blended teaching only where facilities, network, and teacher support meet its high requirements
description: The article's limitations section states that "smart classrooms have high requirements in terms of classroom facilities and network speeds" and that "if the requirements cannot be met, many teaching designs cannot be implemented". It also notes the combined design "place[s] a higher burden on teachers". The principle is therefore to secure the facility, network, and staffing preconditions — and to share the load — before adopting the design, rather than assuming any classroom can host it.
requirements: Classroom facilities and network speeds sufficient for the smart-classroom teaching designs
Teachers able to comprehensively use the information technology involved, including virtual simulation training systems, the PAL app, and Rain Classroom
constraints: The article recommends establishing an efficient and cooperative teaching team with clear task distribution and cooperation with information technology companies to reduce the teacher burden
The study was conducted at a single university in Henan Province with a limited sample size, so the authors call for large-scale verification
target_learners: Undergraduate nursing students
target_learning_goals: Academic performance in basic nursing courses
Independent learning ability
examples: The article suggests that more schools be equipped with smart teaching tools given the reported teaching effect, and that teaching teams cooperate with information technology companies to improve platform digital functions

article_title: Leveraging e-Learning technology to enhance pre-service training for healthcare trainees in Ghana: evidence from a pilot project and pointers to policy reforms.

BMC Health Services Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12913-021-07224-3
title: SMART e-Learning pilot project: a Moodle-based platform with offline WLAN content delivery for pre-service health trainees
description: The SMART e-Learning pilot was inaugurated on 24 May 2018 at the University of Health and Allied Sciences, Ghana, enrolling 675 students, faculty and ICT personnel on Moodle with over 15 undergraduate and postgraduate courses mounted. "The SMART e-Learning pilot project entailed provision of learning content (e-books, links to database articles, distribution of course updates); communication from lecturers to students (sharing lecture materials/resources, academic announcements); online/offline assessments (quizzes, assignments, case scenarios, case studies which are all timed & secure, self-test, scoring component), and creation of discussion for a (students can communicate with lecturers & peers, and interact as a class or in groups) for students and teaching faculty." It delivered materials free of charge through students' existing mobile devices.
requirements: ICT infrastructure set-up and capacity building for teaching and ICT staff, as in the project's five implementation phases
constraints: End of semester examinations were not written via the Moodle platform because the university was yet to adopt an e-Learning policy for university-wide examinations
target_learners: pre-service healthcare trainees (nursing, midwifery, public health nursing, radiology) in a public university
target_learning_goals: access to learning materials, interim assessments, assignment submission, and lecturer-student communication
examples: The pilot ran in SONAM and SAHS across the first and second semesters of the 2018/2019 academic year and was evaluated by a census survey of enrolled students.

title: Provide proper guidelines for smartphone use at home and in school to raise awareness of smartphone addiction's adverse academic effects
description: The article recommends that, given high rates of smartphone dependence among adolescents, "proper guidelines on smartphone use should be provided at home and in school to raise awareness of the adverse effects of SA on students' academic performance." This is a home-and-school awareness guideline grounded in the study's finding that SA significantly predicted low PAP. It works by informing students, parents, and educators about problematic use patterns and addiction risk.
requirements: Awareness of students' smartphone use patterns and addiction levels among parents and educators
Coordination between home and school settings in communicating the guidelines
constraints: The supporting evidence is cross-sectional, so causal effects of SA on academic performance cannot be determined
Results come from a convenience sample of Filipino high school students and may not generalize
target_learners: High school students (grades 7–12)
target_learning_goals: Protecting academic performance from problematic smartphone use
examples: The study surveyed 3374 Filipino junior and senior high school students via an online Google Forms survey and found 62.4% had smartphone addiction, with SA significantly predicting low PAP

description: E-learning materials developed by five dental hygiene educators, covering "resin restoration, inlay restoration, crown restoration, root canal treatment and fillings, and tooth extraction".
